findings.title: Global cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: This line changes the main cleanup loop from every 10 minutes to every 1 minute. It affects every job registered in clean(), including dashboard versions, snapshots, expired images, query history, and annotation cleanup. The PR is aimed at reducing MySQL lock contention in annotation cleanup, but running all cleanup work 10x more often can significantly increase database load and may worsen lock contention. This unrelated behavior change should be reverted or explicitly justified.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level with full ID lists
findings.body: r.log.Error is used after fetchIDs succeeds (and similarly after deleteByIDs at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), even though err is nil on every successful path and the code logs the entire ids slice plus the generated condition. Cleanup runs on a schedule and can process many batches, so this floods logs with error-level entries and large ID lists during normal operation. These should be Debug-level logs, or the ID lists should be omitted.

findings.title: deleteByIDs can exceed bind-parameter limits on non-SQLite databases
findings.body: The new delete-by-ID query builds one placeholder per row ("?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)) and only special-cases SQLite. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above the database bind-parameter limit (for example 65535 on PostgreSQL/MySQL), every cleanup batch will fail with a SQL error. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have a per-batch placeholder limit. The IDs should be chunked on all dialects according to their dialect limits, not only for SQLite.

findings.title: SQLite IN-list construction is quadratic in batch size
findings.body: The SQLite branch builds the IN-list by repeatedly calling values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v), which copies the entire accumulated string for each ID. With a batch size over 999 (the test uses 32767), this causes O(n²) string copying and many large allocations on a hot cleanup path. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join to construct the literal list in linear time.
